finding.technicalSummary: ReadingStatisticsTest.kt has no analog to iOS's `readiumOnlyWorkCountsAsStarted` regression test (KudosTests/ReadingStatisticsTests.swift:67-78), which exists specifically to prevent the 'started' field list from drifting away from the canonical `hasStartedReading`. Given the Android bug reported separately in this review (ReadingStatistics.kt's `hasStarted` omitting the readiumLocator check), a mirrored test would have caught it. There is also no test covering mature-content/privacy filtering in the stats pipeline at all (consistent with that filtering not existing on Android yet, per the separate privacy finding).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The Android test suite is missing a safety-net test that iOS has, which checks that a work is still counted as 'started' even if its only progress signal is the reader's internal bookmark. That gap is likely why the Android bug in this same area went unnoticed.

finding.technicalSummary: CollectionDetailScreen.kt's CollectionWorkRow (lines 208-266) renders `work.title` and `"by ${work.author}"` directly, and shows an always-tappable "Read" button whenever `work.hasEpub`, with zero reference to mature-content privacy settings. The screen's composable signature (lines 41-47) takes only `collectionId` and `workRepository` — no `SettingsRepository`/`PrivacySettings` at all, unlike `LibraryScreen(...)` which takes an optional `settingsRepository` (LibraryScreen.kt:96) and uses `LibraryPrivacy.visibility(work, privacy)` (library/LibraryPrivacy.kt) to blur/obscure mature-rated works via `LibraryCarouselCard`'s `obscured` flag (LibraryScreen.kt:917-970), which also blocks reading until revealed (`canRead = work.hasEpub && !obscured`). iOS's counterpart, `CollectionDetailView`, renders each work through `SensitiveWorkRow(work:, expandAll:, openMode: .reader)` (Collections.swift:155), which blurs title/author and suppresses the reveal until tapped whenever `hideMature && work.isAdult && mode == .obscure && !gate.isRevealed(work)` (MatureContent.swift:109-150). So on Android, any work rated Mature/Explicit that the user has configured the app to hide/obscure everywhere else is shown in full — title, author, and a working Read button — the instant it's viewed via any Collection it belongs to.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If you've turned on "hide mature content," mature works are blurred everywhere in the app — except inside Collections. Opening any collection that contains a mature work shows its full title, author, and a tappable Read button, completely bypassing the privacy setting.

finding.technicalSummary: `deleteCollection()` (CollectionDetailScreen.kt:94-107) calls `workRepository.deleteCollection(collectionId)`, which is implemented in WorkRepository.kt:342-346 as `collectionDao.removeAllWorks(collectionId); collectionDao.deleteById(collectionId)` — an immediate, permanent SQL DELETE with no soft-delete step and no undo. The confirm dialog itself (lines 109-136) even tells the user "The collection is removed. Works stay in your Library" with no mention that this is irreversible or of any recovery window. iOS's equivalent instead calls `PreservedWorkService.softDelete(collection, in: context)` (Collections.swift:254), which sets `isPendingDeletion = true` and schedules permanent removal `recoveryWindow` (90 days) later (PreservedWorkService.swift:44-46, PersistenceSync.swift:274-276) — the collection is recoverable from Recently Deleted (RecentlyDeletedView.swift) until then. Worse, Android's own `RecentlyDeletedScreen.kt` empty-state copy (line 184-185) explicitly promises "Deleted works, collections, and reading queues stay here for 90 days before they're permanently removed" — but `RecentlyDeletedViewModel.state` (RecentlyDeletedScreen.kt:61-63) only ever observes `workRepository.observeRecentlyDeleted(): Flow<List<SavedWork>>` (WorkRepository.kt:57), which never includes collections. Deleted collections never appear there because they're already gone.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Deleting a collection on Android is instant and permanent — there is no 90-day "Recently Deleted" safety net for it, even though the app's own Recently Deleted screen says deleted collections should stay recoverable for 90 days. On iOS, deleting a collection is undoable for 90 days; on Android, one tap and it's gone for good.

finding.technicalSummary: `CollectionDao.getWorksForCollection` (lines 36-45) and `getWorkIdsForCollection` (lines 47-54) join straight against `works`/`collection_work_cross_refs` with no `isDeleted = 0` filter, unlike `WorkDao.getAll()` (WorkDao.kt:31-33) which explicitly excludes soft-deleted works from the main Library with `WHERE isDeleted = 0`. Consequently `WorkRepository.worksForCollection()` (line 299-301) and the `workIds` used to build `WorkCollection` (line 287-296) include works that have been soft-deleted to Recently Deleted. This surfaces as: (1) `CollectionDetailScreen.kt`'s work list (lines 190-202) still shows a soft-deleted work with fully active Read/Remove buttons, and (2) both `CollectionsScreen.kt`'s "N works" badge (CollectionRow, lines 207, 231-236) and `CollectionDetailScreen.kt`'s header subtitle (lines 146-151) count soft-deleted works toward the total. iOS explicitly excludes them: `CollectionCard.workCount` filters `!$0.isPendingDeletion` (Collections.swift:27-28) and `CollectionDetailView.works` filters `!$0.isPendingDeletion` (Collections.swift:128).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: A work you've already deleted (moved to Recently Deleted) can still show up as a normal, fully usable item inside any collection it was in, and it's still counted in that collection's "N works" total — even though it no longer appears anywhere else in your library.

finding.technicalSummary: CollectionDetailScreen's header `trailing` slot (lines 152-162) offers only a "Delete" button; there is no rename action anywhere in the file, and no corresponding call into `WorkRepository`. iOS's `CollectionDetailView` toolbar menu offers a "Rename" item (Collections.swift:219-224) that opens an alert with a `TextField` and commits via `collection.name = trimmed; collection.markModified(); try? context.save()` (Collections.swift:236-247). A collection created with a typo, or one the user simply wants to re-title, can't be renamed on Android at all — the only recourse is delete-and-recreate, which also drops any existing membership unless manually re-added.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: There's no way to rename a collection on Android. If you misspell a collection's name or just want to change it, your only option is deleting it and starting over — which loses which works were in it.

finding.technicalSummary: CollectionDetailScreen has no "Add Works" action; its empty state (lines 182-189) tells the user to "Add works from Work Detail with Add collection" instead. But that reverse path is also degraded: WorkDetailScreen.kt's "Add to Collection" dialog (lines 538-588) only offers a text field to type a collection name (reused case-insensitively via `createCollection`, WorkRepository.kt:307-325) — there's no list of the user's existing collections to pick from or toggle membership in, so adding a work to an existing collection requires retyping its exact name from memory. iOS provides both directions properly: `AddWorksToCollectionView` (Collections.swift:435-568), opened via the collection's own "+" toolbar button (Collections.swift:204-207), lets the user search/multi-select from all eligible library works to add to that collection; and `AddToCollectionView` (Collections.swift:289-400), opened from a work's detail page, shows every existing collection as a row with a checkmark toggle plus a field to create a new one.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: On iOS you can add works to a collection either from the work itself (picking from a checklist of your collections) or from inside the collection (browsing and multi-selecting your whole library). On Android, the only way in is from the work's page, and even there you have to type the exact collection name yourself — there's no list to pick from, and no way at all to add works starting from the collection screen.

finding.technicalSummary: `CollectionWorkRow`'s "Remove" button (line 260-262) calls `onRemove` directly, which wires to `removeWork(work.id)` (lines 78-92) and removes the membership immediately with no confirmation step of any kind. iOS gates the equivalent action behind `@AppStorage("confirmBeforeDelete")` (default `true`): a swipe-to-remove either shows `destructiveConfirmation` (Collections.swift:157-166, 264-273, naming the work and collection) or removes directly only if the user has turned that setting off. Android does define an equivalent `confirmBeforeDelete` setting (SettingsScreen.kt:440, SettingsModels.kt:67) but it is never read anywhere in the app's Kotlin source outside of Settings/backup plumbing — it has no effect on this action (or apparently any action).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Tapping "Remove" on a work inside a collection removes it instantly with no "are you sure?" prompt, even though the app has a "confirm before delete" setting that iOS honors here. A stray tap silently drops a work from its collection, and since there's no existing-collections picker to re-add it (see the other Add Works finding), putting it back means retyping the collection name by hand.

finding.technicalSummary: There is no dedicated collections test file anywhere under android/app/src/test (no `CollectionsTest.kt`, `CollectionDetailTest.kt`, or `WorkRepositoryCollectionsTest.kt`). The only collections coverage is two RoomDaoTest.kt cases (around lines 230-249, 250-280) exercising a basic add-work-then-read-back of `getWorkIdsForCollection`/`getWorksForCollection`. Nothing tests `deleteCollection`'s hard-delete-vs-soft-delete behavior, `createCollection`'s case-insensitive dedup, `removeFromCollection`, or — notably — whether soft-deleted (`isDeleted = 1`) works are excluded from `getWorksForCollection`/`getWorkIdsForCollection` (they currently are not; see the related finding above). A test asserting that soft-deleted works don't leak into collection membership would likely have caught that bug directly.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The automated tests barely touch collections — there's no dedicated test file, and nothing checks that deleting a collection, renaming, or filtering out already-deleted works actually behaves correctly. This is the kind of gap that let the mature-content and deleted-work leaks above ship unnoticed.

finding.technicalSummary: iOS treats "add to a reading queue" and "Save" as two independent flags: ReadingQueueService.addToSavedForLater/addAndPreserveSummary explicitly set `saved.isSaved = false` for a work created solely to satisfy a queue add (ReadingQueueService.swift:300, :550), and AddToQueueView's footer tells the user so ("Queue membership keeps a local EPUB available without marking the work as saved", ReadingQueues.swift:767). On Android, `SavedWork` has no isSaved/isQueued distinction at all — `ensureLocalThen` (WorkDetailScreen.kt:367-380), the helper every reading-queue action (`onAddToSavedForLater` at 646-655, `onAddToQueue` at 656-664) routes through when a work hasn't been imported locally yet, calls `workImporter.saveMetadataOnly(remote)`, which (WorkImporter.kt:25-36) hard-codes `markSaved = true`. `WorkMetadataMerger.merge` then sets `isSaved = base.isSaved || markSaved` (WorkMetadataMerger.kt:53), so the freshly-created row is permanently `isSaved = true`. Symmetrically, `ReadingQueueRepository.removeWork`/`removeFromSavedForLater` (ReadingQueueRepository.kt:75-79, 132-135) only deletes the membership row and never touches the work's saved state or soft-deletes it, unlike iOS's `removeFromQueueAndDeleteIfQueueOnly`/`removeFromAllQueuesAndDeleteIfQueueOnly` (ReadingQueueService.swift:575-600), which is exactly the cleanup counterpart to iOS's isSaved=false-on-create rule.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: On the iPhone app, tapping "Add to Saved for Later" on a work you haven't downloaded yet only queues it for offline reading — it does not add it to your permanent Library. On Android, doing the same thing quietly also marks the work as fully "Saved," so it ends up sitting in your Library forever even after you remove it from the reading queue, which is not what the iOS app does and not what the user asked for.

finding.technicalSummary: iOS never adds a work to a queue without also trying to preserve it: `ReadingQueueService.add` is always called through `addAndPreserve` (ReadingQueueService.swift:248-262) or the summary-based `addAndPreserveSummary`/`addToSavedForLater(_ summary:...)` (lines 264-306, 519-557), both of which call `preserve(work:in:)` (lines 308-369) to download the EPUB via `AO3Client.shared.downloadEPUB` right after creating the membership. Android's `ReadingQueueRepository.addWork` (lines 50-73) and `addToSavedForLater` (122-125) only insert a `ReadingQueueMembership` row — there is no call anywhere in this repository, or at any of its call sites in WorkDetailScreen.kt/LibraryViewModel.kt, to `WorkImporter.download`/`DownloadQueue` when a work is queued. `SavedWork.hasEpub` stays whatever it already was (false for a newly-imported work, since `WorkMetadataMerger` defaults `hasEpub = false` for brand-new rows), so nothing is actually preserved for offline reading until the user separately finds and taps the unrelated "Download" action.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The whole point of a reading queue (like Saved for Later) is that the app should download a local copy so the story is available offline. On iOS, adding a work to a queue automatically starts that download in the background. On Android, adding a work to a queue does nothing but remember that you queued it — no download happens, so the work will not actually be available if you go offline unless you separately go find the download button and tap it yourself.

finding.technicalSummary: iOS's `ReadingQueueDetailView` lets the user rename a custom queue (alert at ReadingQueues.swift:300-311, driven by a plain `queue.name = trimmed` mutation) and delete one (confirmation dialog at 312-326 calling `deleteQueue()` at 468-471, which soft-deletes the queue into Recently Deleted for 90 days), plus drag/VoiceOver reordering of a queue's works (`moveWorks`/`moveWork`/`WorkReorderDropDelegate`, lines 440-530, backed by `ReadingQueueService.reorder`). Android's `ReadingQueueRepository` (this file, all 154 lines) exposes no rename, delete, or reorder method at all — `ReadingQueueDao.deleteQueueById` (ReadingQueueDao.kt:67) exists in the DAO but is never called from anywhere in the app. `ReadingQueuesScreen.kt`'s `QueueRow` and `QueueDetailScreen.kt` have no menu, swipe action, or button offering rename/delete/reorder. Once a user creates a custom queue (via LibraryScreen.kt's "New Queue" tile), there is no way to rename it if mistyped or delete it if no longer wanted, and its work order is fixed at insertion order.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: On iOS you can rename a reading queue, delete one you no longer want (it goes to Recently Deleted, recoverable for 90 days), and drag to reorder the works inside it. On Android none of that exists — once you create a custom queue you're stuck with its name forever, can never remove it, and can't reorder the works in it.

finding.technicalSummary: The only test file for this area covers `ensureSavedForLaterQueue`, `addWork`/`removeWork`/`listWorks` round-tripping, the "missing work" fallback title, and `addToSavedForLater`/`removeFromSavedForLater`. It has no coverage of `createQueue` (dedup-by-name behavior, sort-order assignment), of `sortOrderInQueue` ordering after repeated add/remove cycles, or of `touchQueueMembershipChanged`'s effect on `dateUpdated`/`lastMembershipChangedAt`. This gap tracks with the missing functionality noted elsewhere (no rename/delete/reorder/preservation to test), but the existing `createQueue` logic itself (duplicate-name matching) is also untested.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The automated tests for reading queues only check the basics (add/remove a work, default Saved for Later queue). Creating a custom queue and its ordering logic aren't tested at all, so a regression there wouldn't be caught automatically.

rejected.areaTitle: Recently Deleted / purge of expired soft-deletes

finding.technicalSummary: Android's Work Detail screen binds a Recently-Deleted (isDeleted=true) local match straight into `state.local` and then lets ordinary actions mutate it without reviving it first. `hydrateFromAo3WorkId` (WorkDetailScreen.kt:156-166) and the `WorkDetailSource.RemoteSummary` branch (WorkDetailScreen.kt:202-216) both call `WorkIdentityIndex.findExisting`/`workRepository.findBySourceUrl`, neither of which filters `isDeleted`, and adopt whatever they find into `state.local` unconditionally. From there, `toggleSaved()` (WorkDetailScreen.kt:399-412) — reached whenever `state.local != null` — does `workRepository.upsert(local.copy(isSaved = !local.isSaved, lastModifiedAt = Instant.now()))`, which never touches `isDeleted`/`deletedAt`/`permanentDeletionScheduledAt`. The same is true of `ensureLocalThen` (WorkDetailScreen.kt:367-380), used by Save-for-Later/Add-to-Queue: when `state.local` is a soft-deleted record it runs the action directly on it (e.g. `readingQueueRepository.addToSavedForLater(work.id)`), again without reviving. iOS's counterpart is explicit about the opposite behavior: `resolveExistingIfNeeded` (WorkDetailView.swift:561-574) deliberately does NOT adopt a Recently-Deleted match ('A match sitting in Recently Deleted is deliberately not adopted'), and every mutating action instead routes through `withLocalWork` (WorkDetailView.swift:604-613), which explicitly checks `if work.isPendingDeletion { PreservedWorkService.restore(work, in: context) }` before running the action — documented as a persistence invariant. Net effect on Android: re-opening a soft-deleted work (e.g. tapping the same AO3 link, search result, or series entry again — the work is still 'Saved' so it still shows as normal) and tapping Save, Save-for-Later, or Add-to-Queue updates local flags and reports success in the UI, but the work stays `isDeleted=true`, remains excluded from `observeSavedWorks()`/the Library, and stays on schedule for permanent purge in `sweepExpiredSoftDeletes()`.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If you delete a work and then come across it again later (by tapping the same AO3 link or search result) and try to Save it, add it to a reading queue, or save it for later, the app acts like it worked — but the work actually stays hidden and still scheduled to be permanently deleted in 90 days. The user gets no warning that anything is wrong.

rejected.areaTitle: Recently Deleted / purge of expired soft-deletes

finding.technicalSummary: Where Android's revival logic does fire — `WorkMetadataMerger.merge()` clearing `isDeleted`/`deletedAt`/`permanentDeletionScheduledAt` when `existing.isDeleted == true` (WorkMetadataMerger.kt:39, 82-84), used by `WorkImporter.saveMetadataOnly`/`download` and reached from the everyday 'Save' button (WorkDetailScreen.kt:245-253) — it never retracts the `SyncTombstone` recorded at soft-delete time, and never bumps `lastModifiedAt` either (the `base.copy(...)` in WorkMetadataMerger.kt omits `lastModifiedAt`, so it stays at the original deletion timestamp). `WorkRepository.upsert()` (WorkRepository.kt:87-90), which this path calls, does not retract tombstones — only `restoreFromRecentlyDeleted()` (WorkRepository.kt:175-187, via `retractWorkTombstone` at 252-254) does that. `DownloadQueue.isAlreadyDownloaded()` (DownloadQueue.kt:240-253) works around this for its own call site only, and its comment explicitly says so: '...restoreFromRecentlyDeleted also retracts the soft-delete's sync tombstone, which the WorkImporter-side revival fixes for the redownload paths don't (they have no repository access to do so).' Consequence: `BackupMergeService.suppressesWorkResurrection` (BackupMergeService.kt:742-758) suppresses an incoming work when `tombstone.lastModifiedAt >= archivedWork.lastModifiedAt`. Since a merger-revived work keeps `lastModifiedAt` pinned at the original soft-delete instant (same instant the tombstone recorded), a subsequent backup export/import onto a new device (or merge with a second device) will treat the tombstone as authoritative and silently drop the now-active, revived work forever — even though it's alive and visible on the originating device. iOS's `PreservedWorkService.restore` (PreservedWorkService.swift:70-77) always retracts the tombstone and is called unconditionally by the revive-on-any-interaction path in `importEPUB` (WorkImporter.swift:39-40) and `ReadingQueueService.addToSavedForLater`; this is explicitly asserted by `PreservedWorkTests.swift` (`addToSavedForLaterRevivesRecentlyDeletedWork`, line 262; `importEPUBRevivesRecentlyDeletedRecordInsteadOfDuplicating`, lines 266-291), which Android's test suite has no equivalent of.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: When you delete a work and then re-save it later (not through the explicit Restore button), the app correctly brings it back into your Library on this device — but it leaves behind an internal 'this was deleted' marker that never gets cleaned up. If you later back up your library and restore it on a new phone (or sync with another device), that leftover marker can cause the work to silently vanish again on the new device, permanently, with no indication anything went wrong.

rejected.areaTitle: Recently Deleted / purge of expired soft-deletes

finding.technicalSummary: iOS's `PreservedWorkService` soft-deletes three record types — `SavedWork`, `WorkCollection`, and `ReadingQueue` — each getting the same 90-day recoverable window in `RecentlyDeletedView`/`sweepExpired` (PreservedWorkService.swift:44-52 for collections, 58-66 for queues; confirmed by the delete confirmation copy in Collections.swift:249-260, 'The collection moves to Recently Deleted for 90 days...', and ReadingQueues.swift:313-323, 'The queue moves to Recently Deleted for 90 days...'). Android's `WorkRepository` only implements soft-delete/restore/sweep for `SavedWork` (softDelete/restoreFromRecentlyDeleted/sweepExpiredSoftDeletes, WorkRepository.kt:157-227). `deleteCollection()` (WorkRepository.kt:342-346) is an immediate, unconditional hard delete (`collectionDao.removeAllWorks` + `collectionDao.deleteById`) with no tombstone recorded and no path back — its own confirm dialog says only 'The collection is removed. Works stay in your Library.' (CollectionDetailScreen.kt:94-136), with no mention of recovery because none exists. Reading queues have no delete affordance in the Android UI at all (`ReadingQueuesScreen.kt`, `QueueDetailScreen.kt`) — `ReadingQueueDao.deleteQueueById` exists but nothing in the repository or UI layer calls it, so queue deletion isn't reachable yet. Meanwhile Android's own `RecentlyDeletedScreen.kt` empty-state and header copy (lines 161, 184-186) explicitly promises 'Deleted works, collections, and reading queues stay here for 90 days before they're permanently removed' — text that is currently false for collections (permanently gone the instant you confirm) and moot for queues (can't be deleted yet).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Deleting a work gives you 90 days to change your mind, same as on iPhone. But deleting a collection (a shelf you made to organize works) is instant and permanent on Android, with no way to undo it — even though the app's own 'Recently Deleted' screen claims collections get the same 90-day safety net that works do. On iPhone, deleting a collection is just as recoverable as deleting a work.

finding.technicalSummary: Android's entire `author` package is one file, `AuthorWorksScreen.kt`, which does nothing more than run an AO3 creator-name search (`AO3AuthorUrls.worksSearchUrl` -> `work_search[creators]=<name>`) and render the resulting `AO3SearchPage` in a Previous/Next-paginated `LazyColumn` of `AO3WorkCard`s. It is reached only from `WorkDetailScreen`'s tappable author-name text via `AppNavHost.kt:394-413`, passing a bare display-name `String` (no username/pseud identity is ever captured — `AO3WorkSummary.authors: List<String>` in network/ao3/search/AO3SearchModels.kt:8 stores only text scraped by `h4.heading a[rel=author]`, never an href). iOS's counterpart, `AuthorProfileView.swift` (backed by `AO3AuthorProfileModel`/`AO3AuthorProfileService`), is a full profile screen built on a real `AO3AuthorRoute(username, pseud)`: a hero card (avatar, join info, subscriber counts), Subscribe / Mute / Block actions gated on login (`subscriptionTapped`/`moderationTapped`, lines 335-356), a pseud switcher when the author has multiple pseuds (`pseudSelector`, lines 203-244), four content tabs — Works, Series, Bookmarks, About (bio + pseud list + account info) — implemented in `AuthorProfileContentSections.swift` (`AO3AuthorWorksSection`, `AO3AuthorSeriesSection`, `AO3AuthorBookmarksSection`, `aboutRows`), a fandom filter chip strip for the Works tab (`AO3AuthorFandomFilterSection`), bulk work selection, an 'Open on AO3'/Share/'Select Works' overflow menu, and a stale-cache banner. None of this exists on Android: no Series tab, no Bookmarks tab, no About/bio, no Subscribe/Mute/Block, no pseud disambiguation, no fandom filter. Android also can't distinguish two different AO3 accounts that happen to share a pseud display name, since it navigates by raw text rather than a resolved user/pseud route.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: On iOS, tapping an author's name opens a real profile page: their bio, a Subscribe/Mute/Block button, and separate tabs for their Works, Series, and Bookmarks. On Android, tapping an author's name just runs an AO3 search for that name and shows a plain list of their works with Previous/Next buttons — there's no bio, no subscribe button, no series list, no bookmarks, and no way to pick a specific pseud if the author writes under more than one name. A user coming from the iOS app would find the Android author page dramatically thinner.

finding.technicalSummary: There is no test file for `AuthorWorksScreen.kt` itself under android/app/src/test/java/io/github/cidy02/kudos/author/ (the directory doesn't exist). The only related test coverage is network/ao3/author/AO3AuthorUrlsTest.kt (URL building) and works/AuthorTapNamesTest.kt (author-name extraction from a work). The screen's own state machine — Loading/Loaded/Error transitions, the `load(page)` retry-with-same-page path, and the Previous/Next enabled/disabled bounds in `PaginationRow` — has no unit or Compose UI test exercising it.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The code that drives the author-works screen's loading, error, and page-navigation states isn't covered by any automated test, so a regression there (e.g. Retry loading the wrong page, or the Next button staying enabled past the last page) wouldn't be caught before release.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: Android's reader theme is independent of the app-wide Material theme: `ReaderSettingsMapper.resolveTheme` (reader/settings/ReaderSettingsMapper.kt:40-54) branches on `reader.matchAppReaderTheme`, and `ReaderViewModel.setColorTheme` (reader/ReaderViewModel.kt:116-127) explicitly persists `matchAppReaderTheme = false` the moment a user picks a theme from the in-reader Display sheet, so from then on the reader theme (Light/Sepia/Dark, mapped to Readium's `Theme` in readium/ReadiumSettingsAdapter.kt:24-28) can legitimately differ from the app's own `KudosThemeMode` (ui/theme/Theme.kt). Despite this, `ReaderPageSkeleton` (ui/components/ReaderPageSkeleton.kt:62) paints its background with `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.background` — the app-wide theme color — and `ReaderScreen`'s outer `Surface` (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:97) does the same. Even at the second skeleton state where the theme IS already known (`ReaderUiState.Reading.preferences.theme`, shown at reader/ReaderScreen.kt:150 while the EPUB file opens), that data is never passed to `ReaderPageSkeleton`. This is precisely the bug class iOS fixed this session: iOS's `ReaderOpeningSkeleton`/`ReadiumReaderView` deliberately use `themeManager.readerTheme.backgroundColor` (SkeletonLoading.swift:270-275; also ReadiumReaderView.swift:471/497/505) instead of `.systemBackground`, specifically because the app theme and reader theme can diverge and a mismatched background flashes on open.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If you pick a reader theme (say Sepia) that's different from your overall app theme (say Light), every time you open a book the screen will briefly flash the app's Light background before switching to the Sepia reading page. iOS just fixed this exact flash; Android still has it.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: Android sizes the opening skeleton with a fixed heuristic — `bodyLines = ((screenHeightDp - 160) / 28).coerceIn(8, 18)` (ui/components/ReaderPageSkeleton.kt:55-57) — rather than measuring the actually available height and filling it, as iOS's `ReaderPageSkeleton.paragraphs(filling:)` does (SkeletonLoading.swift:228-260, with `ReaderPageSkeletonTests.swift` pinning both the no-overflow and no-underfill invariants). The 18-line cap means content stops growing once `screenHeightDp` exceeds ~664dp; on many current phones (`screenHeightDp` commonly 800-950dp) this leaves several hundred dp of visible blank space between the last skeleton line and the floating 'Opening…' caption at the bottom of the screen — the exact 'lines stopped well short of the bottom' symptom the iOS test suite's docstring says was the original owner-reported bug. Conversely the 8-line floor forces a minimum line count regardless of how little height is actually available (e.g. Android split-screen/multi-window or a foldable's small window), so on a sufficiently short window the lines (laid out in a non-scrolling `Column`, ui/components/ReaderPageSkeleton.kt:67-96) can run past the bottom edge.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: On many modern, tall phone screens the opening-book skeleton's placeholder text lines stop well short of the bottom of the screen, leaving an odd empty gap — the same look-broken symptom iOS just fixed. In a split-screen or very short window it can go the other way and the lines can run off the bottom instead.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: iOS's reader chrome top bar (`ReaderChromeTopBar.swift:56-100`) shows a two-line title pill: the work title plus an author line underneath (person glyph + `state`'s author). Android's `ReaderTopBar` (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:267-319) only takes and renders a `title: String` parameter (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:293-299) — it never receives or shows `state.work.author`, even though `SavedWork.author` (core/model/SavedWork.kt:9) is readily available at the call site (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:204-213 passes only `title = state.work.title`). The reader's top bar drops the author entirely.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: iOS shows the book's title and its author under the back button while reading. Android's reader header shows only the title — the author's name is missing.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: iOS's reader has a fully wired text-to-speech feature (`ReaderSpeechController.swift` 810 lines + `ReaderSpeechPreferences.swift`/`ReaderSpeechSettingsSection.swift`/`ReaderSpeechSkip.swift`, ~1287 lines total, added 2026-07-29 and exposed as a 'Read Aloud' action, `ReadiumReaderView.swift:1238`). Android's reader package has no speech/TTS code anywhere (`grep -rl "speech\|Speech\|TTS"` under the reader package returns nothing), and `ReaderTopBar` (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:267-319) exposes no such action. This is a real, substantial capability gap, but it is already tracked as a known P2 backlog item in the Android repo's own TASKS.md ('Text-to-Speech (TTS) — large; AVSpeechSynthesizer in the reader'), so it is not a hidden regression — flagging for completeness since TTS was explicitly in scope for this review.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: iOS can read a book aloud to you in the reader; Android has no read-aloud feature at all. This is already on the Android team's own to-do list, not a surprise bug, but it's worth confirming it's still the plan.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: iOS's Customize Theme sheet (`CustomizeThemeView.swift`) offers a live-rendered preview, a font picker (incl. custom fonts), Bold Text, a master 'Customize' toggle, and sliders for Line Spacing / Character Spacing / Word Spacing / Margins plus Justify Text and a Reset button. Android's equivalent, `ReaderDisplaySheet` (reader/ReaderScreen.kt:394-443), exposes only a font-size-percent slider and a theme picker; `ReaderViewModel` (reader/ReaderViewModel.kt) has no setters for line height, letter/word spacing, margins, justify, bold, or font family — even though `ReaderPreferences` already carries all of these fields (reader/settings/ReaderPreferences.kt) and most (line height, margins, justify) are already mapped through to Readium's `EpubPreferences` in `ReadiumSettingsAdapter.toEpubPreferences` (reader/readium/ReadiumSettingsAdapter.kt:22-39) — they just have no UI path to be changed by the user. This is explicitly acknowledged as deferred in the repo's own docs/ai/HANDOFF.md ('full reader settings UI remain incomplete') and TASKS.md, so it's a known gap rather than a silent regression.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: iOS lets you fine-tune the reading page in detail — font, bold, line/letter/word spacing, margins, justified text, with a live preview and a reset button. Android's version only lets you change text size and the light/sepia/dark theme; the rest of the customization options aren't available yet. This is already a known, tracked gap on the Android side.

rejected.areaTitle: Reader: EPUB rendering, chrome, themes, TTS, customize panel, open/loading skeleton

finding.technicalSummary: iOS pins its skeleton's fill arithmetic with a dedicated `ReaderPageSkeletonTests.swift` that exercises `ReaderPageSkeleton.paragraphs(filling:)` as a pure, internal (non-private) function across a range of heights, specifically to catch overflow/underfill regressions like the one this review found analogous evidence for (Finding: `bodyLines` clamp gap/overflow). Android's `bodyLines` calculation (ui/components/ReaderPageSkeleton.kt:55-57) is inline inside the `@Composable` function rather than factored into a standalone testable function, and there is no test file for `ReaderPageSkeleton` under android/app/src/test/java/io/github/cidy02/kudos/ (confirmed via directory search) despite the rest of the reader package (progress mapping, TOC builder, view model prefs, settings mapper) being well covered by JVM unit tests.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The logic that decides how many placeholder lines to draw while a book is opening has no automated test on Android, unlike iOS which specifically tests this after finding bugs in it. Worth adding a test once the fill logic above is fixed.

finding.technicalSummary: AO3WebLoginScreen's WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading guards navigation with `!request.url.host.orEmpty().endsWith(AO3Constants.WORKS_HOST)`, i.e. a bare `endsWith("archiveofourown.org")` with no domain-boundary check. That allows any host that merely ends with the literal string, e.g. `evilarchiveofourown.org` or `xarchiveofourown.org`, to load inside the login WebView (shouldOverrideUrlLoading returns false = let it load) — the malicious host is a strict superstring, not a real subdomain. Every other AO3-host check in this codebase gets this right by requiring a dot before the suffix: AO3CookieJar.kt:24 (`normalized.endsWith(".${'$'}{AO3Constants.WORKS_HOST}")`), AO3Session.kt/AO3StoredCookie.isAO3Domain:49 (same pattern), and iOS's AO3RequestDefaults.isTrustedURL in AO3AuthService.swift:213 (`host.hasSuffix(".archiveofourown.org")`). Only this one call site is missing the leading dot, so it's an inconsistency within the same codebase, not a deliberate design choice.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The login screen's check for 'is this still an AO3 page' can be tricked by a domain that simply ends with the letters 'archiveofourown.org' with nothing separating them, like 'evilarchiveofourown.org' — it isn't required to be a real archiveofourown.org subdomain. If an attacker ever got the login page to redirect there, the app would treat it as trusted and let it render full-screen inside the login flow, which is exactly the kind of check that's supposed to stop that.

finding.technicalSummary: AO3AuthRepository.restoreSession() calls `sessionStore.load()` (line 33) with no try/catch around it. FileAO3SessionStore.load() (AO3SessionStore.kt:24-35) only catches IllegalArgumentException and SerializationException around `sessionFile.readText()` — a plain IOException (e.g. MalformedInputException from a partially-written/corrupted file, a permission error, or a disk I/O failure) is not caught and propagates out of restoreSession(). restoreSession() is invoked from AccountViewModel.kt:28 as `viewModelScope.launch { authRepository.restoreSession() }`, which also has no try/catch, so an uncaught IOException here crashes the app on launch. iOS's equivalent restoreSession() (AO3AuthService.swift:401-428) wraps the whole `vault.load()` call in a do/catch that maps every error (not just deserialization errors) to a safe `.signedOut` state with a message, and even has a dedicated recovery path for a missing-Keychain-entitlement error.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If the saved-login file on disk is ever unreadable for a reason other than being garbled JSON — a permission glitch, a disk error, a half-written file from a previous crash — the Android app will crash every time it starts, instead of just showing the user as logged out like the iPhone app does in the same situation.

finding.technicalSummary: In AO3WebLoginScreen's onPageFinished (lines 88-103), the JS inspection result is only acted on when `inspection.loggedIn && inspection.username != null`; if loggedIn is true but the `#greeting a[href^='/users/']` scrape fails to find a username (markup change, A/B variant, edge case), the branch is simply skipped — no call to acceptWebLogin, no error message set, no state change. The screen just sits there, fully loaded, silently never completing. Because this is Android's *only* login path (a plain visible AO3 WebView, with no native username/password form), there is no independently-known username to fall back to. iOS's equivalent (AO3WebLoginCoordinator.swift:189-194, `completeAuthentication(username: observation.username ?? expectedUsername)`) always has a fallback: the username the user actually typed into the native form (`hiddenExpectedUsername`/`manualExpectedUsername`), so an AO3 markup gap there degrades gracefully instead of stalling.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If AO3's page changes in a way that makes the app unable to read the username off the logged-in page, the Android login screen will just sit there forever after the user successfully logs in on AO3's own page — no error, no progress, nothing — because unlike the iPhone app it has no other way to know who just logged in. The user would be stuck and have no idea why.

finding.technicalSummary: Neither AO3AuthTest.kt nor AO3SessionRestoreTest.kt directly exercises AO3AuthRepository.acceptWebLogin() (blank-username validation branch, cookieStore.captureSession() returning null branch, or the success path's state/persist side effects) or AO3AuthRepository.sessionDidExpire(). AccountLogoutTest covers logout() via restoreSession()+logout(), but the web-login-completion and mid-session-expiry entry points — both real, non-trivial branches in AO3AuthRepository.kt — have no direct unit test.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The code path that actually finishes a login (after the user submits AO3's web form) and the code path that reacts to AO3 kicking the session out mid-session don't have their own automated tests, even though the surrounding session-restore and logout logic does.

finding.technicalSummary: Android's CommentsScreen (Loaded branch, lines 110-172) renders only the composer, an optional status message, a divider, and the flat comment list. It never renders the work's title, author, fandom, rating, chapter count, or total-comment count anywhere on screen, and the surrounding Scaffold's TopAppBar always shows the static string "Comments" (Routes.titleFor in app/Routes.kt line 86; wired in app/MainScaffold.kt line 63) with no work-specific subtitle. iOS's CommentsView.infoSection (CommentsView.swift lines 390-457) renders a card with work title (title3/semibold), author byline (tappable, opens profile), fandom label, and a stats row (rating/chapters/total comments) as the first row of the List, in addition to the plain "Comments" nav title. AO3CommentThread/AO3Comment on Android also carry no work-title/author/fandom fields at all (network/ao3/comments/AO3CommentModels.kt lines 45-59), so there is no data available to render this even if the UI were added.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: When you open Comments on Android, the screen never tells you which work you're looking at — no title, no author, no fandom — just "Comments" at the top and a bare list. On iOS the same screen shows a card with the work's title, author, and fandom right above the comments. If you navigate to Comments from different works in quick succession, or forget which work you tapped into, there's no way to confirm you're commenting on the right one without leaving the screen.

finding.technicalSummary: CommentsScreen's onSubmit (lines 124-147) and AO3CommentRepository.submitComment (network/ao3/comments/AO3CommentRepository.kt lines 45-92) perform a single POST with no idempotency/duplicate-submission protection: on any AO3Result.Failure the draft text is preserved in the text field, `submitting` resets to false, and the Post button re-enables — there is no distinction between a definitive rejection (e.g. validation error, safe to retry) and an ambiguous outcome (timeout / connection-drop after the POST reached AO3, where the comment may already have been recorded). A user who sees an error after a timeout and taps Post again can create a genuine duplicate live comment on AO3. iOS solves exactly this with CommentSubmissionGuard + CommentsModel.submit/reverify (CommentsModel.swift lines 1035-1147): it single-flights POSTs, classifies ambiguous errors (isAmbiguousSubmitError), blocks resubmission until an explicit verification GET confirms absence, and persists that block across screen recreation (see KudosTests/CommentSubmissionTests.swift, the whole file). None of this exists on Android — there's no verification call, no ambiguous-state UI, and no submission guard/store.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: If posting a comment on Android times out or the connection drops partway through, the app just shows a generic error and lets you tap "Post Comment" again with the same text — but the first attempt may have actually gone through. That risks posting the same comment twice to a public work page, and since the app has no way to edit or delete a comment afterward, you'd have to go to the AO3 website to clean it up. iOS specifically guards against this by checking with AO3 before allowing a retry.

finding.technicalSummary: CommentRow (CommentsScreen.kt lines 221-241) only ever displays comment.depth as static indentation — there is no per-comment action of any kind (no Reply button, no tap target). CommentComposer (lines 176-219) only ever posts through repository.submitComment(target, draft), and AO3CommentRepository.submitComment (AO3CommentRepository.kt lines 45-92) has no parentCommentID/context parameter at all; every submission goes to target.defaultSubmitUrl() as a new top-level comment. So a user can view nested replies (via depth-based indent) but has no way to reply to a specific comment — threading is read-only. iOS's CommentsModel.startComposer(replyingTo:) (CommentsModel.swift line 940) and the reply/edit submit path (CommentsModel.swift lines 907-936, postCommentReply) let the user tap Reply on any comment, quote it in the composer, and post a properly-threaded child comment.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: You can see that comments are nested replies to each other (the indentation shows it), but there's no way to actually reply to a specific comment on Android — the only option is posting a brand-new top-level comment on the whole work. On iOS, tapping Reply on any comment posts your response nested under it, exactly like AO3 itself does.

finding.technicalSummary: AO3CommentTarget.pageUrl() (AO3CommentModels.kt lines 12-39) never adds a `page` query parameter, and AO3CommentRepository.loadThread (AO3CommentRepository.kt line 23) only ever calls it once with no page argument — so only AO3's first comments page is ever fetched. AO3CommentThread (lines 45-50) carries no totalPages/totalComments/currentPage fields, and CommentsScreen has no pagination UI or "there are more comments" indicator. For any work whose comment count exceeds one AO3 page, the app silently shows an incomplete list with no way to reach the rest. iOS's CommentsModel tracks page/currentPageNumber/totalPages (CommentsModel.swift lines 82-83, 601-665) and CommentsView renders an explicit Previous/Next pagination control (CommentsView.swift lines 631-707) whenever page.totalPages > 1.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Android only ever loads the first page of a work's comments and has no page controls, so on a work with a lot of comments you'll only ever see the first batch with no indication that more exist or any way to reach them. iOS shows a Page X of Y control so you can browse the whole thread.

finding.technicalSummary: CommentRow renders every comment identically regardless of authorship, with no edit/delete affordance and no data path to do so — AO3CommentRepository has no editComment/deleteComment methods and AO3Comment (AO3CommentModels.kt lines 52-59) carries no editPath/deletePath fields. iOS exposes both via swipe actions wired through CommentThreadHandlers.onEdit/onDelete (CommentsView.swift lines 369-376) and CommentsModel.startEditing/deletableComment (CommentsModel.swift lines 994-1012), plus a confirmation alert and delete() call (CommentsView.swift lines 875-896).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Once you've posted a comment on Android, you can't edit or delete it from within the app — you'd have to go to the AO3 website. iOS lets you swipe on your own comment to edit or delete it directly.

finding.technicalSummary: CommentRow displays `Text(comment.author.name, ...)` as plain, non-interactive text (line 227). AO3CommentAuthor.profileUrl (AO3CommentModels.kt line 63) is parsed by AO3CommentParser (line 67) but never read anywhere in the UI layer, so there is no way to open a commenter's AO3 profile from the Comments screen. iOS renders the author name/avatar as a tappable control that opens the author's profile (CommentAuthorAvatarButton / onOpenAuthor, wired through CommentThreadHandlers in CommentsView.swift).
finding.plainEnglishSummary: Commenter names on Android are just plain text — tapping one does nothing, even though the app already knows the link to their profile. On iOS, tapping a commenter's name opens their AO3 profile.

finding.technicalSummary: AO3CommentRepositoryTest.kt and AO3CommentParserTest.kt cover: public/authenticated load, empty-body validation, a single successful top-level POST, and one AO3 validation-error response. There are no tests for a network timeout / connection-drop during submitComment (the ambiguous-outcome case iOS's whole CommentSubmissionTests.swift suite exists to cover), no tests for multi-page comment threads, and no tests for reply/edit/delete flows — consistent with those code paths not existing yet in AO3CommentRepository.
finding.plainEnglishSummary: The automated tests for Android's comment posting only check the happy path and one error page — there's no test coverage for what happens on a network timeout during posting, or for replies, editing, deleting, or multi-page comment threads, mirroring that those features aren't implemented yet.
